input.question: How closely and with how much detail could astronomers see Jupiter in the 17th century?
input.ground_truth: Obviously this was before photography was invented, but many of these early telescopic astronomers did leave us drawings of their views of Jupiter: - Galileo Galilei left [these drawing from 1610 detailing the positions of Jupiter's moons](_URL_0_). Not much is seen of Jupiter itself other than a disc. - Robert Hooke, generally credited with discovering the Great Red Spot, had a better telescope and made [this drawing of Jupiter in 1666](_URL_2_). - Giovanni Cassini had a considerably better telescope than either. [Here are some of his drawings from 1665, 1672, and 1677.](_URL_1_)

response.prediction:
Okay! Imagine you have a big, shiny marble that's really far away. That marble is Jupiter, and a long time ago, in the 1600s, people wanted to look at it with their telescopes (which were like super-powered glasses).

Back then, the telescopes weren't as strong as the ones we have now. So, people could see that Jupiter was a round ball, not a star. They could also see that it looked a little bit fuzzy and maybe saw some tiny dots next to it—those were Jupiter’s four big moons, which Galileo found!

But they couldn’t see all the pretty stripes and swirls on Jupiter like we can today. It kind of looked like a fuzzy, round ball with some little friends (the moons) near it. They couldn’t see the storms or the details, just the basics.

So, they could see that Jupiter was special and different from the stars, but not all the cool details we see now.
